<reason>Both sides argued cleanly around a real structural question: does the extra agency paperwork attached to vouchers create a legitimate landlord-side burden distinct from tenant qualification, or does a categorical refusal of that paperwork simply function as a proxy exclusion of a protected class? CON built a consistent analytic distinction (contract obligations vs. identity-based proxies) and used a good concrete hypothetical (the mortgage-deadline landlord), but never quantified the burden and, crucially, never fully answered PRO's "nullity" challenge: if "standard program terms" is a permissible reason to refuse, any landlord can dress up blanket exclusion as "declining contract terms," which would gut the rule entirely. PRO's rebuttals were sharper and more responsive: the "split security" reply to the partial-voucher point, the observation that CON's own proposed remedy (streamlined approvals) requires continued landlord engagement rather than a right to refuse altogether, and especially the closing move turning CON's own words in [A4.6] ("uniform effect... without resting on judgment about character") into an admission that the policy operates as a class-based exclusion. CON's answer to that in the closing reasserted the distinction rhetorically ("standard terms are still terms") without new argumentative traction. PRO's opening being clipped for exceeding the word limit is a real execution flaw and cost against it, but the lost material was minor framing language, not substantive support, so it does not offset PRO's stronger rebuttal work and cleaner final framing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's use of CON's own [A2.6]/[A4.6] language — that the disputed term "applies to every participant" and produces a "uniform effect" — to reframe CON's defense as a confession of proxy discrimination was the most decisive turn; CON's closing never fully neutralized it, instead repeating the contract/identity distinction without resolving PRO's "nullity" charge.</best_rebuttal>
